checked.issues: Key supported: NHS Jaundice page opened (jaundice needs urgent GP/111 assessment, can signal serious liver disease); BNF opened (Budd-Chiari syndrome, benign hepatocellular adenoma and hepatocellular carcinoma are contra-indications; gallbladder disease a caution; hepatic impairment: avoid in acute disease or liver tumour). CKS COC topic opened (Last revised in August 2024) but not cited. No live pill+jaundice duplicate. Key was the shortest option (72 vs 96-104); lengthened to 101 (second-longest, not the longest). Added the BNF statement and NHS review date to why_correct. KEY SHORTEST: yes in draft, no after fix.

options.A: Same-day medical assessment with liver blood tests and ultrasound imaging of the liver and bile ducts
options.B: Reassure her that these are recognised minor effects of the pill and arrange a routine review next month
options.C: Change to a different brand of combined pill and ask her to report back if the symptoms continue
options.D: Advise simple analgesia and rest, with the symptoms to be reviewed at her next scheduled pill check
options.E: Prescribe a course of oral antibiotics for a presumed urinary tract infection and review in a week

edits.correct_answer: A. Same-day medical assessment with liver blood tests and ultrasound imaging of the liver and bile ducts
edits.why_correct: Jaundice with severe upper abdominal pain suggests a significant liver or biliary problem and needs prompt assessment with liver function tests and imaging; it should not be put down to the pill. Combined hormonal contraceptives are linked with conditions such as gallbladder disease, Budd-Chiari syndrome and liver tumours, which make them contraindicated or cautioned, so the pill should be reviewed urgently and usually withheld while the cause is found (the BNF advises avoiding combined hormonal contraceptives in acute liver disease or liver tumour). NHS advice is that jaundice needs urgent medical assessment. Source: BNF, Ethinylestradiol with levonorgestrel (contra-indications, cautions and hepatic impairment); NHS.uk, Jaundice (page last reviewed 22 January 2024).

NG257 also offers serum progesterone for prolonged irregular cycles (1.18.8) but it is not an option. Prolactin/thyroid/rubella statements match 1.18.11, 1.18.12, 1.20. Chlamydia antibody testing is not in NG257 (tubal assessment is HSG/HyCoSy), so why_wrong C softened. options.B: Serum CA125 to screen for endometriosis
options.C: Chlamydia antibody testing to assess tubal damage
options.D: Thyroid peroxidase antibody level to look for autoimmunity
options.E: Serum rubella IgG to confirm her immunity status

edits.correct_answer: A. Serum gonadotrophins (FSH and luteinising hormone)
edits.why_correct: Irregular cycles point towards an ovulatory disorder, so NICE advises measuring serum gonadotrophins (FSH and LH) in women with irregular cycles who are being investigated for infertility. Because her cycles are prolonged as well as irregular, serum progesterone is also offered; prolactin is added only if an ovulatory disorder, galactorrhoea or a pituitary tumour is suspected. Source: NICE NG257, Fertility problems: assessment and treatment, 2026.
edits.why_wrong: B. CA125 is not used to diagnose endometriosis, and she has no pelvic pain to suggest it. C. Chlamydia antibody testing is not part of the NICE-recommended tubal assessment (hysterosalpingography or hysterosalpingo-contrast-ultrasonography), and tubal damage would not explain unpredictable cycles. D. Thyroid antibodies are not routine; thyroid function is checked only if she has symptoms of thyroid disease. E. Rubella immunity is a pre-conception check and does not explain a delay in conceiving.

edits.why_correct: Pregnancy is best planned when lupus is quiet, and some medicines, including mycophenolate, are harmful in pregnancy and must be changed before conception, whereas hydroxychloroquine is usually continued. A planned review with the rheumatology team allows medicines to be adjusted and specialist antenatal care to be arranged. Source: NHS.uk, Lupus (page last reviewed 19 July 2023); BNF, Mycophenolate mofetil (pregnancy: avoid unless no suitable alternative) and Hydroxychloroquine sulfate (may be continued in pregnancy).

edits.stem:
A 16-year-old girl has had cramping pelvic pain with every period since she was 13, and it has worsened each year. She now misses school for two or three days each month, and ibuprofen and paracetamol only partly help. She is not sexually active, and her abdominal examination is normal.

Which diagnosis should be suspected?

CKS: start on day 1 (immediate cover) or first 5 days; any other time with pregnancy reasonably excluded, barrier method for 7 days (9 days for Qlaira); no doubling of dose. Stem uses a standard pill. No live duplicate (missed pills/vomiting/antibiotics items differ). Explanations clean. KEY SHORTEST: no (78 of 74-81).

Key supported by sources I opened: NHS 'Side effects and risks of the combined pill' (blood clots in leg or lung; slight increase in breast and cervical cancer; pill lowers ovarian cancer risk; page last reviewed 15 February 2024), NHS 'What is the combined pill' (fertility returns about a month after stopping), BNF (increased risk of venous thromboembolism in CHC users). The draft cited a 404 NHS URL and a BNF treatment summary that does not carry the claim, so the Source line is replaced. No live duplicate (PAQ840 is Factor V Leiden; DVT items are diagnosis). Caveat: stroke and breast cancer are also serious effects but are not offered. KEY SHORTEST: no (54 of 50-56).

edits.why_correct: Oestrogen-containing combined hormonal contraception increases the risk of venous thromboembolism (deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism), even in healthy young women. The absolute risk is small, but it is the key serious adverse effect to explain, and she should be told to seek urgent help for unilateral calf swelling or sudden breathlessness. Source: NHS.uk, Combined pill: side effects and risks (page last reviewed 15 February 2024); BNF, Ethinylestradiol with levonorgestrel (risk of venous thromboembolism).
